content.title: About
content.content: A chimichanga is a deep‑fried Mexican dish consisting of a flour tortilla filled with meat, cheese, vegetables and beans. The tortilla is folded, sealed and fried until golden and crispy, creating a crunchy, flavorful snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chimichangas originated in the American Southwest, where Mexican cuisine blended with Native American cooking traditions.
Traditional fillings include black or pinto beans, which add protein and make the dish more filling.
In the United States they are often served with salsa, guacamole and sour cream.
The dish can be baked, but deep‑frying gives it the characteristic crunch.
Vegetarian versions replace meat with mushrooms, tofu or extra beans.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans in the filling provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from beans and vegetables supports digestion and promotes lasting satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Legumes and whole‑grain tortilla supply B1, B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Beans contribute iron, magnesium and potassium, which help heart and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and spices (paprika, cumin) are rich in antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: High fat content when fried
items.content: Deep‑frying increases calories and saturated fat, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beans, experiencing skin or digestive reactions.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Prepared sauces can raise salt content; control added salt for a healthier option.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Undercooked beans may contain antinutrients; ensure beans are fully cooked before assembling.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the chimichanga hot, cut in half. It can be eaten alone or with salsa, guacamole, sour cream and fresh herbs. For a lighter version bake it in the oven, then drizzle with a little olive oil before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chimichangas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. They can also be frozen for up to 2 months; reheat in the oven to restore the crisp crust.

content.title: About
content.content: A classic frozen mixed vegetable blend typically includes carrots, peas, corn, green beans, and sometimes broccoli. The vegetables are blanched, flash‑frozen, and a small amount of vegetable oil is added to improve flavor and mouthfeel. The product is ready to eat after heating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetables are frozen shortly after harvest, preserving most of their vitamins and minerals.
The blend is commonly used in quick dishes such as stir‑fries, soups, and side dishes.
Added fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
Frozen vegetables can be stored up to 12 months without quality loss when kept properly.
The mix is often sold in portion‑controlled bags for home and commercial kitchens.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Carrots and peas provide vitamin B6, which supports protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots and lutein from corn help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, essential for vision.

items.title: Improves fat‑soluble vitamin absorption
items.content: The added oil aids the uptake of vitamins A, D, E and K.

items.title: Allergy to individual vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may react to peas or corn.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain versions may contain added salt; check the label if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Caloric contribution from fat
items.content: Added oil increases the product’s calorie count; portion control is advised.

items.title: Texture loss if overheated
items.content: Overcooking can make the vegetables mushy and watery.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the mix in a skillet, microwave, or steamer until hot. Season with herbs, soy sauce, or a sprinkle of cheese for variety. It works as a standalone side or as part of dishes such as pasta, rice, omelets, and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, use within 3–4 days while maintaining a constant frozen temperature. Do not thaw and refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit croissant is a pastry that combines a classic flaky croissant dough with a fruit puree or fresh fruit filling. The dough is made from flour, butter, eggs and yeast, while the filling may include apple, cherry, strawberry or exotic fruits. The product offers a crisp, layered texture together with a bright fruit flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fruit croissants appeared in France in the early 1920s as a variation of the traditional croissant with seasonal fruits.
The flaky dough is created using the "turning" technique, repeatedly folding and rolling the dough with butter.
Fruit fillings are often cooked with a touch of sugar and cinnamon to enhance aroma.
In some regions the croissant‑fruit is finished with a light dusting of powdered sugar or a glaze.
Vegan versions replace butter with plant‑based margarine and eggs with a vegan binder.

items.title: Source of vitamins
items.content: The fruit filling provides vitamin C, vitamin A and B‑vitamins, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fruits add dietary fiber that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in trans‑fats
items.content: When prepared correctly, the flaky dough contains minimal trans‑fats, which is better for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Fruits are rich in antioxidants (polyphenols, carotenoids) that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The croissant‑fruit provides quick energy from the carbohydrates in the dough and fruit.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The dough contains wheat, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit filling and added sugar can increase calories and affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Fruit acidity
items.content: Acidic fruits (e.g., cherry) may irritate the stomach lining in individuals with high acidity.

items.title: Trans‑fat formation
items.content: If baked at excessively high temperatures, trans‑fats may form, which are undesirable in the diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fruit croissant warm, straight from the oven. It can be enjoyed as a snack, paired with coffee or tea, or used in dessert plates together with ice cream or whipped cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fruit croissants in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage refrigerate up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat in the oven for 5‑7 minutes before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli cheese soup is a thick, creamy soup made from fresh broccoli, cheese (usually cheddar or parmesan), vegetable broth, and cream. It has a mild aroma, a slightly sweet broccoli flavor, and a rich cheesy finish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli is often called "little trees" because its florets resemble tiny crowns.
Broccoli‑based soups are popular in diet plans due to low calories and high nutrient density.
Cheese is typically added at the end of cooking to preserve its flavor and texture.
In Italy a similar dish is known as "Zuppa di Broccoli al Formaggio" and is served with croutons.
Broccoli provides over 100% of the daily value of vitamin C per 100 g.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains calcium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals from the cheese contribute to bone and teeth health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Broccoli provides glucoraphanin, which converts to sulforaphane, a potent antioxidant.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium in broccoli helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared soup often contains added salt; those with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Broccoli may cause gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: High oxalate levels in broccoli can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often topped with croutons, grated cheese, and fresh herbs. It can be stored in the refrigerator and reheated, or frozen for longer keeping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared soup in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for 2‑3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving.
